title: An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge
focus: the mind's final escape at the moment of death

teacherSummary.text: Peyton Farquhar, a Southern planter, stands on a railroad bridge in Alabama about to be hanged by Union soldiers. Part II flashes back: a disguised Union scout tempted him to try burning the bridge. In Part III the rope seems to break; he swims, dodges bullets, and walks all night to his home, where his wife waits. As he reaches for her, a blow falls: he is dead, his body swinging beneath the bridge.

discussionQuestions: Time can feel slow or fast. When has a moment seemed to last forever?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this story is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge,” how does Bierce show the mind's final escape at the moment of death? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the structure you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge, how does Bierce develop the idea of the mind's final escape at the moment of death? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the structure in the story helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge (where it begins, turns and ends) and its structure shape the reader's understanding of the mind's final escape at the moment of death. writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge suggests about the mind's final escape at the moment of death. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the story's structure and point of view), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Ambrose Bierce uses structure in An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge to complicate the reader's understanding of the mind's final escape at the moment of death. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge within its historical and literary context and argue how the story's treatment of the mind's final escape at the moment of death responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the story's handling of the mind's final escape at the moment of death follows or bends those conventions, using the structure as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge and its treatment of the mind's final escape at the moment of death. State your method, show what it reveals in the story's structure and point of view, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge as evidence for a larger claim about the mind's final escape at the moment of death in An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge. Connect close reading of the story to the whole story, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge as a hinge in the story's larger treatment of the mind's final escape at the moment of death. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge.

satQuestions.passage: The man who was engaged in being hanged was apparently about thirty-five years of age. He was a civilian, if one might judge from his habit, which was that of a planter. His features were good—a straight nose, firm mouth, broad forehead, from which his long, dark hair was combed straight back, falling behind his ears to the collar of his well-fitting frock-coat. He wore a mustache and pointed beard, but no whiskers; his eyes were large and dark gray, and had a kindly expression which one would hardly have expected in one whose neck was in the hemp. Evidently this was no vulgar assassin. The liberal military code makes provision for hanging many kinds of persons, and gentlemen are not excluded.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Time can feel slow or fast. When has a moment seemed to last forever? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board. Before we start, a content note: Heads-up: this story includes execution by hanging; Civil War violence.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are engulfed, pitilessly, inhaled, smashing, carpeted. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “He felt his head emerge; his eyes were blinded by the sunlight; his chest expanded convulsively, and with a supreme and crowning agony his lungs engulfed a great draught of air, which instantly he expelled in a shriek!” In this sentence it means: swallowed up completely. Word histories: For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge would have known. Bierce fought for the Union at Shiloh and Chickamauga; the story (1890) is in Tales of Soldiers and Civilians. Why does this story matter? A celebrated experiment with time and point of view; the twist depends on shifting from objective to subjective narration. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for structure.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “The man who was engaged in being hanged was apparently about thirty-five years of age.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to the mind's final escape at the moment of death? I circle “assassin”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find structure, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for structure.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of structure. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: The man who was engaged in being hanged was apparently about thirty-five years of age. He was a civilian, if one might judge from his habit, which was that of a planter. His features were good—a straight nose, firm mouth, broad forehead, from which his long, dark hair was combed straight back, falling behind his ears to the collar of his well-fitting frock-coat. He wore a mustache and pointed beard, but no whiskers; his eyes were large and dark gray, and had a kindly expression which one would hardly have expected in one whose neck was in the hemp. Evidently this was no vulgar assassin. The liberal military code makes provision for hanging many kinds of persons, and gentlemen are not excluded.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Structure, Point of view, Imagery: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge develops the idea of the mind's final escape at the moment of death. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of structure and point of view shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions (focus set for the class level): wait time, think-pair-share on DOK 3/4, follow-up probes.
segments.script: Let's talk. We move from what happens to why it matters to whether it's right. After each question I wait before calling on anyone: think first. Our anchor question: How does this story connect to illusion and reality? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

segments.activity: Story quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the story quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this story suggests about the mind's final escape at the moment of death, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how structure shapes the mind's final escape at the moment of death. Tonight, read the next story and add two words to your etymology log.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.
